name: Clonazepam
mechanism: Enhances GABA-A receptor activity by increasing frequency of chloride channel opening. Produces anxiolytic, anticonvulsant, sedative, muscle relaxant effects. Long-acting benzodiazepine. Suppresses seizure spread and focal epileptic activity
dosing: Epilepsy: start 250mcg (0.25mg) nocte, increase by 250mcg every 3-7 days. Usual maintenance: 4-8mg daily in 2-3 divided doses (max 20mg/day). Panic disorder: start 250mcg BD, increase to 1mg BD after 3 days (usual range 1-4mg/day). Elderly/hepatic impairment: start 250mcg nocte, cautious titration. Gradually taper when stopping (reduce by 250mcg every 1-2 weeks) to avoid withdrawal
contraindications: Respiratory depression, acute pulmonary insufficiency, severe hepatic impairment, sleep apnoea, myasthenia gravis (worsens muscle weakness). Caution: elderly (falls, confusion), hepatic/renal impairment (accumulation), history of substance abuse (dependence risk), depression (disinhibition, suicidality)
interactions: CNS depressants (alcohol, opioids, antipsychotics, antihistamines, Z-drugs) ↑ sedation, respiratory depression (avoid/use cautiously). CYP3A4 inhibitors (erythromycin, fluconazole, ritonavir) ↑ clonazepam levels. CYP3A4 inducers (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin) ↓ levels. Sodium oxybate: severe respiratory depression (contraindicated). Baclofen, tizanidine: ↑ sedation/muscle relaxation
monitoring: Sedation level, cognitive impairment (memory, attention). Dependence (especially >4 weeks use). Signs of withdrawal if stopping (anxiety, tremor, seizures). Seizure frequency (epilepsy). Mood, suicidal ideation (paradoxical effects possible). Falls risk (elderly). Respiratory rate (especially with other depressants). LFTs if hepatic impairment
pregnancy: Avoid if possible - benzodiazepines associated with cleft lip/palate (first trimester, small ↑ risk), neonatal withdrawal, floppy baby syndrome. Use only if benefit outweighs risk. If essential for epilepsy, continue (uncontrolled seizures greater risk). Taper before delivery if possible. Neonatal monitoring if used near term
sideEffects: Very common: drowsiness, fatigue, dizziness, ataxia, cognitive impairment (memory, concentration). Common: depression, confusion, muscle weakness, blurred vision, hypersalivation. Paradoxical reactions (especially children, elderly): agitation, irritability, aggression, disinhibition. Dependence (physical/psychological - develops within 2-4 weeks). Withdrawal: anxiety, tremor, insomnia, seizures (if abrupt cessation). Respiratory depression (especially with other CNS depressants). Falls (elderly). Tolerance (anticonvulsant effect may diminish)
pharmacokinetics: Well absorbed orally (90%). Peak 1-4h. Highly protein-bound (85%). Metabolized hepatically to inactive metabolites (not CYP-dependent, mostly nitro-reduction). Half-life: 20-40h (long-acting - once/twice daily). Excreted renally (metabolites). Accumulates in elderly/hepatic impairment
clinicalPearls: Brand: Rivotril. LONG-ACTING benzodiazepine (half-life 20-40h). Uses: epilepsy (focal, absence, myoclonic seizures), panic disorder, acute mania (off-license), REM sleep behavior disorder (off-license). EPILEPSY: third-line for most seizure types (tolerance common). Useful for myoclonic seizures, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Often used as adjunct. Tolerance develops - may lose efficacy over time (anticonvulsant tolerance, but anxiolytic effect persists). PANIC DISORDER: effective but dependence limits long-term use. Prefer SSRIs first-line. Clonazepam for acute/refractory cases. DEPENDENCE: develops rapidly (2-4 weeks). Difficult withdrawal - requires slow taper (250mcg reduction every 1-2 weeks, slower if symptoms). Withdrawal can cause rebound anxiety, insomnia, seizures (even if no epilepsy history). NEVER stop abruptly if on >4 weeks. ELDERLY: high falls risk (sedation, ataxia, muscle weakness). Avoid if possible. Start very low dose (250mcg nocte). COGNITIVE EFFECTS: impairs memory, concentration, reaction time (warn re driving, machinery). May worsen dementia. ALTERNATIVES: epilepsy - levetiracetam, lamotrigine (less tolerance). Panic disorder - SSRIs, CBT. Insomnia - CBT-I, short-term Z-drugs (less dependence than benzos). OVERDOSE: supportive care, flumazenil (benzodiazepine antagonist - caution in epilepsy, may precipitate seizures). Respiratory depression with co-intoxication (alcohol, opioids). DRIVING: impairs coordination, reaction time - DVLA advise patients. May need to inform DVLA if sedation persists. DURATION: avoid long-term if possible (<4 weeks). If chronic use essential (epilepsy), accept dependence but don't abruptly stop
indication: Epilepsy (myoclonic seizures, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, absence seizures refractory to first-line). Panic disorder (short-term or when SSRIs ineffective). Acute mania (adjunct). REM sleep behavior disorder (off-license)
